newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian slide toll rises, survival tale emerges.
newsitem.headline: Australian slide toll rises, survival tale emerges.

text.p: The death toll in the Australian ski resort landslide rose to nine on Sunday as rescuers brought in police sniffer dogs to search the twisted ruins for 10 people still missing.
Rescuers have been buoyed by the miraculous survival tale of ski instructor Stuart Diver, pulled from beneath the rubble on Saturday after three days trapped in a concrete tomb.

But attempts to find more survivors beneath the ruins of two ski lodges at the Thredbo Alpine Village, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney, were frustrated on Sunday by fears of further slippages in rubble.

"It's extremely dangerous...," police superintendent Charlie Sanderson told reporters. "The big fear that we have at the moment is that the weather might break. If it rains, that area would be so much more dangerous."
Police said work at the site was interrupted several times overnight as rubble continued to shift ominously.
One huge boulder moved several centimetres and one of the large concrete slabs under which more victims were believed to be entombed slipped just before sunrise.
"There has been some concern about the stability of the site," police spokesman Allan Small told Reuters. "The movement of some rocks and boulders has been giving some anxiety."

Rescuers are now working in two locations in the mangled heap of concrete, twisted metal, dirt and splintered trees, one in which they hope to find more survivors and another where they are recovering bodies.

Rescuers have dug 16 metres (52 feet) of tunnels under the concrete slabs which trapped Diver, believing the area contains crushed bedrooms of one of the lodges, and therefore, may reveal survivors. Diver and his wife, who died in the landslide, were in bed when the mountain gave way, crushing their lodge.
Rescuers are now crawling through the tunnels, digging by hand in a desperate attempt to find another cavity which may have saved some of the initial 20 people buried.
But while rescuers hope for another miracle, the stench and constant reminder of death is ever present on the site.
Rescuers located two more bodies overnight and another on Sunday, bringing the death toll to nine.

Wearing face masks against the stifling smell of death, rescuers recovered two more bodies from the rubble on Sunday, bringing to six the number of victims recovered. Three bodies still remain trapped. Police have declined to identify the dead.
Still missing in the debris was Diver's wife, Sally.
Diver has told rescuers of his amazing survival and how he desperately tried to save his wife.
As underground water filled the cavity in which Diver and his wife were trapped, the fit ski instructor tried to hold his wife's head above water.
But Sally was pinned on a mattress beside him by something heavy and a sudden rush of water ripped her from Diver's grip.
Diver constantly pressed his nose against the concrete slab above his head to breath, as water and mud flooded his tomb, fearing he too would drown.
A fireman heard Diver's muffled voice near dawn on Saturday but rescuers, digging by hand so as not to dislodge the concrete slabs, took 12 hours to free him.
Diver was sandwiched between thick wedges of concrete in a cramped air pocket 10 metres (33 feet) beneath the surface for three freezing nights.
Finally, 64 hours after the landslide hit, Diver was pulled from the wreckage, but miraculously he only suffered lacerations and hypothermia to one toe.
Diver is recovering in a hospital in Canberra, 150 km (90 miles) north of Thredbo, and is reported to be sitting up in bed, in good spirits.
He was expected to remain in hospital for at least a few days for "extensive treatment", a hospital spokesman said.
